meeting_header:
Date: 2027-03-19
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54m
Attendees: Sarah Nguyen (Redwood AE), Tom Reyes (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Polaris CTO), Mateo Ruiz (Platform Eng), Elena Park (Security)
summary: Intro discovery on integrating Redwood across hosted/dedicated/private modes. Discussed LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy patterns, per-route rate limits and quotas, observability hooks (tracing, token-level cost), and security/compliance requirements. Agreed to send pilot pricing and run a private on-prem demo with infra next week.
topics: Rate limits, per-route quotas, burst capacity
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Sarah (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sarah from Redwood, with Tom from our SE org. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya (Polaris CTO): Hi Sarah, hi Tom. Doing well. We've been looking at a couple of inference vendors, want to understand how Redwood would plug into our stack.
[00:12] Tom (Redwood SE): Great. Today we'll focus on the integration side — SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway patterns, rate limits, and observability so you can validate against your infra.
[00:20] Mateo (Platform Eng): Quick context — we're running a mix of server-side agents built on LangChain, some LlamaIndex-based retrieval pipelines, and a small fleet of sidecar proxies in front of our microservices. Mostly GKE and a dark onprem site for regulated customers.
[00:35] Elena (Security): From security, primary questions are around private deployments, KMS integrations, audit logs, and RBAC.
[00:42] Sarah: Perfect — that maps well to Redwood's product lines. We'll cover hosted API and transition paths to dedicated and private. If it's okay, Tom will kick into some architecture patterns.
[00:50] Tom: Cool. So at a high level, integration options are: 1) Direct SDK calls to the hosted Redwood API from your backend, 2) A gateway/proxy — either our lightweight onramp sidecar or your existing API gateway that forwards to Redwood, 3) Self-hosted Private deployment inside your VPC or on-prem for regulatory isolation.
[01:10] Mateo: For the LangChain agents, we currently use an HTTP wrapper that translates chain calls into OpenAI-compatible requests. Would we need to change much?
[01:18] Tom: Not much — our SDK supports an OpenAI-compatible interface and also has first-class helpers for LangChain and LlamaIndex. We have a repo with examples: https://drive.google.com/redwood-langchain-examples (link shared). The wrapper can swap endpoints and minimal headers.
[01:36] Priya: Does Redwood support streaming and function/tool calling the same way? We rely on streaming for user-facing agents.
[01:44] Sarah: Yes — streaming is supported across hosted and dedicated. For private deployments streaming depends on your networking config but it's supported. Function calling is supported in SDKs; Tom has a sample later in the deck.
[01:55] Mateo: About the gateway approach — we've patched in a sidecar that handles things like rate limiting, auth, and request shaping. How would Redwood's gateway integrate?
[02:03] Tom: Two approaches: a) Use your sidecar as a pass-through and call Redwood's hosted/dedicated endpoints directly from it; b) Deploy Redwood's onramp proxy as a sidecar which adds prefix/KV caching, batching, and quota enforcement before requests hit Redwood. The onramp also exposes observability hooks to emit traces and token accounting.
[02:25] Elena: If we used hosted with our sidecar, how do we get audit logs and key management? We need KMS integration and the ability to rotate keys under our control.
[02:33] Sarah: For hosted we provide encrypted at rest, customer keys via external KMS with BYOK in the roadmap (we can share the private deployment KMS flow now). For strict KMS control and full audit logs, Private is recommended — it lets you run the control plane in your VPC and integrate with HSM/KMS and SAML/SSO.
[02:50] Priya: Ok. Cost and latency — our SLO is <120ms 95 p50 for short prompts, 90 tokens on average, and we target cost per 1k tokens to be under $0.80 for retrieval-augmented responses. How does Redwood help with predictions and batching?
[03:07] Tom: We do workload profiling — our runtime picks kernels depending on seq length and auto-batches within latency SLOs. You can configure batching windows and per-route latency targets in Redwood Console. For cost you'll get token-level breakdowns in the console and we recommend quantized model variants on Dedicated/Private for cheaper perf.
[03:27] Speaker 1 (Priya, off mic): Sorry, quick question — you mentioned KV cache, does that work across chains?
[03:34] Tom: The KV cache is at the model runtime level — it caches recurrent K/V tensors for autoregressive decoding and prefix caching for repeated prompt prefixes which helps in multi-agent setups where prompts share common instructions. It's transparent to LangChain, but we also have an SDK helper to manage user-level prefix caches.
[03:50] Mateo: About quotas — we need per-route quotas and per-team rate limits, and quota bursting for spike days. Do you support token-based quotas or just request-based?
[03:59] Sarah: Redwood supports both. You can set per-route token quotas, per-api-key quotas, and burst windows. Rate limits can be enforced at gateway-level or inside Redwood for hosted and dedicated. In Private you can fully customize enforcement.
[04:12] Elena: For compliance, we need immutable audit logs that show who called which model and the token counts. Can logs be pushed to our SIEM?
[04:20] Tom: Yes — audit logs can be streamed to your logging endpoints (e.g., Splunk/Datadog) and include token accounting, api_key, model version, region, and latency. In Private, logs never leave your network. Hosted supports log forwarding but may contain redacted content depending on retention settings.
[04:38] Priya: How does Redwood handle fallback when a region is congested? We need graceful degradation.
[04:45] Sarah: Smart routing policies let you prefer low-latency region but fallback to a cheaper or compatible model variant in a different region. We support canary/fallback policies per route and rollouts can be automated with health checks.
[04:58] Mateo: Integration with LlamaIndex — we use vector stores and a retrieval layer, then pass top-k contexts to models. Any recommended patterns?
[05:07] Tom: Keep retrieval separate; use our embeddings endpoint to generate vectors, or bring your own embeddings. For LlamaIndex we provide a connector that handles batching and automatic embedding calls with backpressure. Also consider using prefix caching for common retrieval contexts to reduce tokens.
[05:22] Sarah: I'll note the example Tom mentioned; we'll include the LlamaIndex connector and a LangChain agents example in the follow-up.
[05:28] Priya: One more — observability: what hooks are available? We need traces spanning service->gateway->model, per-token cost, and per-prompt perf histograms.
[05:36] Tom: We emit distributed traces compatible with OpenTelemetry, per-request traces include model runtime timings, kv cache hits, batch window waits, and tokens emitted. We also export metrics (histograms/counters) for token counts, latency, error rates, and cost attribution. The Console surfaces per-route token breakdowns and you can attach spans to your traces.
[05:56] Elena: Are sensitive fields redacted in logs? We need PII handling.
[06:01] Tom: We have redaction hooks client-side in the SDK so you can redact before it leaves your environment; on Private deployments you can configure automatic redaction policies. Hosted has configurable retention and masking.
[06:15] Priest-alike (Priya): (laughs) That's a new one.
[06:18] Sarah: (laughs) Good.
[06:21] Priya: Thinking about rollout — we want to run a pilot for 4 weeks, with a canary at 5% traffic, then 25%, then 100% if latency and cost metrics hold. How do you support canarying?
[06:31] Tom: Our rollouts support weighted traffic splitting per route, and automatic rollback thresholds on latency and error rate. You can tie rollouts to model versions. For Dedicated we can reserve burst capacity so your canary doesn't get throttled.
[06:45] Mateo: Regarding SDKs — languages? We mostly use Node and Python.
[06:49] Sarah: Official SDKs for Python, Node, and Go. Community SDKs for Java and Rust. We also provide Dockerized onramp templates and Helm charts for sidecar deployment.
[06:58] Mateo: Any rate limiting libraries we should plug into? We currently use envoy rate-limiting ext.
[07:04] Tom: Envoy works fine; you can use envoy with the rate limit service calling Redwood to get quota decisions, or let Redwood enforce quotas internally. For token-aware rate limiting you might prefer Redwood's enforcement since it knows tokens per request.
[07:20] Priya: For private deployment sizing — what's the typical GPU profile for our expected load? We'll send traces but ballpark?
[07:27] Tom: Ballpark depends on model size and qps. For 100 qps with 90 tokens average and target <120ms using a 7B model quantized on A100-like or L4, you'd need a small pool — but we should run a perf benchmark. We can run a short benchmark from your traffic traces in our eval cluster.
[07:48] Mateo: Are there tenancy models for Dedicated? We want strict isolation vs soft-isolation.
[07:53] Sarah: Dedicated offers both: dedicated GPU pools (customer-only) with network isolation. Private gives you full control. Hosted is multi-tenant. We'll include the dedicated SKU and security matrix in the follow-up.
[08:05] Elena: For RBAC, can we map to our SSO roles?
[08:09] Tom: Yes — SAML/SCIM provisioning and role mapping are supported for Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports SSO and RBAC as well but provisioning flows may be slightly different.
[08:20] Priya: I'm curious about quota enforcement at the route level — do you support per-model and per-route quotas simultaneously?
[08:27] Tom: Yes — quotas are multi-dimensional. You can enforce per-route token limits, per-model consumption caps, and global org-level budgets. Policies can be combined, with priority ordering and emergency overrides for SRE.
[08:41] Sarah: Quick note — we have an internal product doc that maps quota primitives to typical policies, we'll attach it.
[08:48] Mateo: A little worried about cold starts if we have many small models pinned to different tenants. How does Redwood mitigate warmup?
[08:56] Tom: We do prewarming for pinned model versions and keep minimal reservations for high-priority routes. For Dedicated/Private you can pin model instances. There's a tradeoff between cost and warm readiness; our optimizer suggests keepalive vs pay-per-warm choices.
[09:12] Priya: On the language model side, do you host open models only or do you support customer-provided weights?
[09:18] Sarah: Hosted catalog is curated open models; Dedicated/Private allows you to bring your model weights (BYOM) under certain licensing constraints. We'll share the onboarding checklist for BYOM.
[09:29] Mateo: About billing — do you do token-level metering for pilot? We need per-team cost centers.
[09:35] Sarah: Token-level billing and per-api-key cost attribution is built in. Redwood Console shows per-route and per-token cost, and you can export cost reports. For pilots we usually offer a committed monthly credit and then usage-based billing.
[09:50] Speaker 2 (Priya): We also run agents that open files and call external tools — any pattern for function calling with LlamaIndex?
[09:58] Tom: Use function-calling features in the SDK; for LlamaIndex, wire a tool executor so results from tools are passed back into the chain. We have an example that integrates function calling with agent loops — we'll include that code snippet.
[10:10] Priya: Can Redwood run inside our air-gapped environment?
[10:14] Sarah: Yes — Private on-prem option supports air-gapped installs. It requires an initial approved image transfer and an offline licensing handshake. We have compliance engineers who run that onboarding.
[10:26] Elena: For the audit trail, do you keep full request/response in logs, or is content redacted by default?
[10:33] Tom: By default hosted retains token counts and metadata; content retention is configurable. We can do full content retention for Dedicated under contract but often redact content for security. Private gives you full policy control.
[10:47] Mateo: Let's talk sample timelines — we want to pilot in 2 weeks and go to production in 8-12 weeks. Is that realistic?
[10:56] Sarah: Yes — typical pilot is 2-4 weeks for integration and performance checks, then 6-8 weeks for production rollouts including security review and procurement. We'll support with an onboarding playbook.
[11:07] Priya: Ok, for the pilot success criteria — we'll define: 95p latency <120ms for short prompts, cost per 1k tokens < $0.80, correct function calling behavior for agents, and no major security gaps.
[11:18] Sarah: Sounds good — we'll capture that as agreed success criteria in the follow-up.
[11:23] Tom: One gotcha: if you use proxy sidecar and let it do token accounting, ensure clocks are synced and headers are passed intact for tracing. We sometimes see dropped x-request-id headers which breaks trace joins.
[11:36] Mateo: Noted.
[11:38] Priya: Anything else on integration?
[11:40] Sarah: A couple more specifics — we'll provide a small test harness that simulates your LangChain flows, and Tom will run a load test with your traces. We'll also provide the Helm chart and envoy config example.
[11:52] Elena: For us security folks, please send the SOC2/ISO posture doc and the private deployment checklist.
[11:58] Sarah: Will do.
[12:00] Speaker 3 (Mateo): One more technical — if we want per-team quotas and showback, can we push cost tags from the SDK?
[12:08] Tom: Yes — SDK accepts metadata/tags on calls that flow to cost reporting. You can tag by team, project, user id. The Console then breaks down costs by tags.
[12:18] Priya: Ok I think that's the main list.
[12:21] Sarah: Great — any blockers on your side for the pilot?
[12:24] Priya: We need to confirm legal and procurement timelines; security will compile questions. Otherwise we can start integration work.
[12:31] Sarah: Awesome. We'll send the pilot packet today.
[12:34] Tom: We'll include a LangChain adapter, a LlamaIndex connector, envoy snippets, and a small load harness.
[12:41] Priya: Thanks both.
[12:43] Elena: Thanks.
[12:45] Sarah: Recap of next steps: Sarah sends pricing + pilot doc; Tom sends code examples and schedules perf test; Priya to send traces and success criteria. We'll meet again for an infra demo on Thursday (2027-03-24).
[12:59] Mateo: Works for me.
[13:02] Sarah: Thanks everyone, end call.
[13:05] -- End of recording --

Notes and links shared in-meeting: https://drive.google.com/redwood-onramp-deck, https://drive.google.com/redwood-langchain-examples, internal: /kb/dedicated-security-matrix (link to be attached in follow-up). The deck includes a sample envoy config and Helm chart.
